headline: White Island Ledge on the Slack: Haddock to 7 Pounds, Stripers Working the Piscataqua Seams
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished all of it — this week the shoals paid, the harbor stripers made you work, and the mackerel showed up right on schedule.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and think New Hampshire's an afterthought between two states with real fishing. I've never seen it that way. Thirteen miles gets you the Piscataqua's cobble bottom and iron current, it gets you Hampton Harbor's sandbars sliding under a boat at half tide, and it gets you six miles out to the Isles of Shoals where the bottom drops into real groundfish structure — ledges, boulder fields, and gullies that fish the same as anything you'd find running two hours from a bigger port. I trailer a 20-foot Lund and I fish this stretch like it's a hundred and thirty miles of coast, because if you know where the rock piles are, it is.

This week that meant mornings at Appledore and White Island before most people had their coffee going. The Gulf of Maine's still running cool enough to keep this a daytime, structure-based program — not the deep, nocturnal grind you're hearing about from the bass south of the Cape where the surface water's pushing into the high 70s and shoving stripers onto wrecks after dark. We flagged that pattern holding steady last week, and up here it has — cooler water, normal tide-and-structure fishing, no need to wait for full dark. Haddock have been the better story on the ledges around White Island and the Appledore backside in 70 to 90 feet, taking clam bellies and diamond jigs tipped with squid strips on the last hour of the ebb into dead slack. Fish to 7 pounds came over the rail Tuesday morning, mixed with pollock and a few keeper cod that wanted the bottom third of the water column, not up in the jig column where the pollock were sitting. If you're marking bait stacked tight to the rock on the sounder, that's your window — the slack, before the current builds back and scatters everything off the structure.

Mackerel showed up in numbers around the Shoals this week too, right on schedule for late July. Diamond jigs and small Swedish Pimples, no bait needed, in 40 to 60 feet over sand pockets between the ledges. They're not just a bonus catch — fresh mackerel strip is about the best haddock bait you can cut yourself, so a lot of guys are jigging a dozen fish first thing and using the rest for bottom rigs the rest of the morning. Simple, cheap, and it works.

Inshore, the striper program has been honest work rather than easy work. Hampton Harbor's been giving up fish on the push tide through the inlet — that first hour and a half of incoming when bait gets funneled past the jetty rocks and stripers stack up to ambush it. Live mackerel and bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig near the rock pile on the north side have produced slot fish to 34 inches, but you need to be there right as the tide turns, because once it's running hard the bite window closes fast and doesn't reopen until the next stage. Rye Harbor's been a flounder spot more than a bass spot this week — small hooks, sandworms, fishing the mud pockets just outside the harbor mouth on the last of the outgoing, nothing huge but steady action for anyone who wants dinner without burning gas.

The Piscataqua's been the most reliable bass water on the beat, which isn't surprising given how much current that river moves. Stripers are holding on the current seams below the Memorial Bridge and around the pilings up toward Portsmouth Harbor, feeding on the tide change rather than blind-casting the whole cycle. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and swung through the seam has been the most consistent presentation — you're imitating a baitfish getting swept out of the eddy, and that's exactly the moment stripers commit. A few bluefish have started mixing in around Odiorne Point and off Great Boars Head, chopping up bait pods close to the rocks in the last two hours of daylight. Nothing like the blitz conditions you're hearing about down on the Jersey and Long Island beaches where warm water's got blues thriving while it pushes bass deep — our water's still too cool for that kind of sustained chaos — but there's enough bluefish showing now that I'd carry a wire leader rig alongside your bass gear if you're working the Boars Head rocks in the evening.

Tide's easing off the last full moon and sliding toward neap over the next several days, which typically softens current speed at the Shoals and on the Piscataqua both. That usually means slightly longer slack windows at the ledges — good news for the haddock and cod program, since a longer slack gives you more time to work a piece of structure before the current builds back. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd plan on hitting White Island or Appledore early, working the slack hard, then coming back inside to catch the tail of the incoming at Hampton Harbor in the afternoon. If a front pushes through midweek like these August systems tend to do, I'd shift days rather than fight a chopped-up ocean six miles out — the groundfish will still be there when it clears.
